CausalChain: PI3K/Akt activation -> induces PTMs on PKM2 -> promotes dimer formation and nuclear translocation of PKM2 -> acts as coactivator for HIF-1α and c-Myc -> upregulates glycolytic and proliferation genes -> enhances aerobic glycolysis and tumor survival -> contributes to sorafenib resistance
Hypothesis: Targeting the post-translational modifications that favor PKM2 dimer formation and nuclear translocation will stabilize its tetrameric, enzymatically active form, thus disrupting the transcriptional activation of glycolytic genes and reversing sorafenib resistance in HCC.
Abstract: Recent studies have elucidated a complex interplay between oncogenic signaling pathways, metabolic reprogramming, and drug resistance in hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC). In particular, the dual functionality of pyruvate kinase M2 (PKM2) — acting both as a glycolytic enzyme and a transcriptional coactivator — establishes a critical link between glycolytic flux and the activation of oncogenic transcription factors. Here, we propose that post‐translational modifications (PTMs) of PKM2, driven by PI3K/Akt signaling, promote its conversion to a dimeric, nuclear form that enhances the transcription of glycolytic and proliferation‐promoting genes, thereby contributing to sorafenib resistance. By stabilizing the tetrameric form of PKM2, it may be possible to not only inhibit excessive glycolysis but also attenuate oncogenic transcriptional programs. This hypothesis paves the way for a novel combined therapeutic strategy targeting both the metabolic reprogramming and transcriptional functions of PKM2 to overcome drug resistance in HCC.
